title: The War Michigan Lost and Won Anyway
description:
In 1835, Ohio and the Michigan Territory raised militias and marched them at each other over a strip of land and the little town of Toledo. There was one "battle", nobody was hit, and the only blood of the whole war came from a penknife held by a man named Two Stickney. Then Michigan lost the war, gave up Toledo, took a frozen wilderness nobody wanted, and found copper in it.

Chapters
0:00 Two armies, one town
0:30 A bad map
1:23 The prize
1:44 The Boy Governor
2:26 The one real battle
2:51 One and Two
3:25 The midnight court
4:05 The deal
5:02 The frozen wasteland
5:36 Who won?

Facts used: the 1787 Northwest Ordinance set the line due east from the southern tip of Lake Michigan; the Mitchell Map, the standard map of the day, put that tip too far north, and Ohio's 1802 constitution bent its border up to the north cape of Maumee Bay if the line fell too far south. Two surveys (the Harris line, 1817, and the Fulton line, 1818) left a strip of about 468 square miles between them. In February 1835 Ohio extended its government over the strip, and six days later Michigan passed the Pains and Penalties Act (fines up to $1,000 or up to five years at hard labor). Michigan's acting governor, Stevens T. Mason, had taken office at 22; Ohio's governor was Robert Lucas. Ohio gathered about 600 militia and Michigan about 1,000. At Phillips Corners in April 1835, Michigan men caught an Ohio survey party and fired shots; nobody was hurt and nine surveyors were arrested. In July 1835, Monroe County deputy sheriff Joseph Wood was stabbed with a penknife by Two Stickney, son of Major Benjamin Stickney (whose other son was named One); the wound was minor, and Ohio did not hand Two over. Local histories also record a horse as the war's only death. On Sept. 7, 1835, the new Lucas County court held a secret session in Toledo by night and fled at a false rumor of Michigan militia. President Jackson removed Mason in August 1835; Michigan voters elected him governor that fall. The act of June 15, 1836 offered statehood for the strip, with the western Upper Peninsula; a convention at Ann Arbor rejected it in September 1836, and the "Frostbitten Convention" accepted it on Dec. 14, 1836, with a share of the federal surplus at stake. Michigan became the 26th state on Jan. 26, 1837. State geologist Douglass Houghton reported copper in the Upper Peninsula in 1841; the rush began in 1843, and Michigan led the nation in copper from 1847 to 1887. In 1973 the Supreme Court (Michigan v. Ohio) settled the Lake Erie boundary in Ohio's favor.

The scenes are an animated dramatization.

comment: So who really won the Toledo War: Ohio, which got its port, or Michigan, which got the copper?
